<|start|>user<|message|>**System Overview**

The model describes a collection of *N* identical concurrent processes that repeatedly try to execute a critical section. The algorithm is a “fast‑mutex” protocol that uses two shared integer registers (`x` and `y`) and a Boolean flag array (`b[1] … b[N]`). Each process also maintains a private control‑flow marker (its “program counter”) that tells which step of the protocol it is currently executing, and a private set `S` that is used while the process is waiting for other processes to clear their flags.

---

### Variables

| Variable | Meaning |
|----------|---------|
| **Program counter (`pc[i]`)** | For each process *i*, this records the current line of the algorithm (e.g., `start`, `l1`, `l2`, …, `cs`). It is used only to drive the state‑transition rules. |
| **`x`** | A shared integer that a process writes with its own identifier when it reaches the “fast‑path” entry point. It is used to detect a race with another process that is also trying to enter. |
| **`y`** | Another shared integer that a process writes with its identifier after setting `x`. It serves as a second “hand‑shake” register that helps decide whether the process can continue or must back off. |
| **`b[i]`** (for each *i*) | A shared Boolean flag that process *i* sets to **TRUE** when it begins the entry protocol and clears to **FALSE** when it either aborts the attempt or leaves the critical section. The flag signals to other processes that *i* is currently in the entry phase. |
| **`S[i]`** (for each *i*) | A private set held by process *i* that initially contains all other process identifiers. While waiting, *i* repeatedly removes from this set any process whose flag `b[j]` has become **FALSE**. When the set becomes empty, *i* knows that all competing processes have withdrawn. |

All variables are initially zero or **FALSE**, and every process starts in the `start` state.

---

### Actions (Steps of the Protocol)

1. **`start` → `l1`** – The process begins a new attempt to enter the critical section.

2. **`l1`** – Sets its own flag `b[i]` to **TRUE** to announce that it is competing for the lock.

3. **`l2`** – Writes its identifier into the shared register `x`.

4. **`l3`** – Checks whether another process has already written a non‑zero value into `y`.  
   *If `y` ≠ 0* the process jumps to step `l4`; otherwise it proceeds directly to step `l6`.

5. **`l4`** – Clears its own flag `b[i]` because it has detected that another process is already in the “fast‑path” region.

6. **`l5`** – Waits until `y` becomes zero (meaning the other process has finished its critical section) and then restarts the whole protocol from `start`.

7. **`l6`** – Writes its identifier into the second shared register `y`.

8. **`l7`** – Compares the value it stored in `x` with its own identifier.  
   *If `x` ≠ i* it means another process wrote to `x` after this process, so it proceeds to the “slow‑path” starting at `l8`.  
   *If `x` = i* the process proceeds directly to the critical section (`cs`).

9. **`l8`** – Clears its own flag `b[i]` (it will now act as a “slow‑path” contender) and initializes its waiting set `S[i]` to contain all other process identifiers.

10. **`l9`** – Repeatedly picks any process identifier `j` that is still in `S[i]` and waits until `b[j]` becomes **FALSE**. When `b[j]` is false, `j` is removed from `S[i]`. This loop continues until `S[i]` is empty, i.e., all competitors have withdrawn.

11. **`l10`** – After the waiting loop, the process checks whether the second register `y` still contains its own identifier.  
    *If `y` ≠ i* it means another process has taken the lock after this process entered the slow‑path, so it goes to `l11`.  
    *If `y` = i* the process can safely enter the critical section (`cs`).

12. **`l11`** – Waits until `y` becomes zero (the other process finishes) and then restarts from `start`.

13. **`cs`** – Represents the critical section. No state change occurs here except moving to the next step.

14. **`l12`** – Upon exiting the critical section, the process resets `y` to zero, indicating that the lock is now free.

15. **`l13`** – Clears its flag `b[i]` and returns to the `start` state to begin another iteration.

All steps are atomic with respect to the model: each transition updates only the variables that belong to the executing process (or the shared variables explicitly mentioned) and leaves everything else unchanged.

---

### Safety Property (Invariant)

The invariant asserts that no two distinct processes can be inside the critical section at the same time. In other words, whenever one process is executing the critical‑section step, every other process must be in some other state of the protocol.

**SAFETY PROPERTY:** *At any moment, it is impossible for two different processes to be simultaneously in the critical section; at most one process may be inside the critical section at a time.*<|end|><|start|>assistant<|channel|>final<|message|>```tla
---- MODULE FastMutexWithGoto2 ----
EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets

\* ---------- Constants ----------
CONSTANT N \* number of processes (set in the cfg)

\* ---------- Derived sets ----------
Proc == 1 .. N

PC == {"start","l1","l2","l3","l4","l5","l6","l7",
       "l8","l9","l10","l11","cs","l12","l13"}

\* ---------- Variables ----------
VARIABLES pc, x, y, b, S

\* ---------- Helper definitions ----------
\* pc[i] : program counter of process i
\* b[i]  : flag of process i
\* S[i]  : waiting set of process i (subset of Proc)

\* ---------- Initial state ----------
Init ==
 /\ pc = [i \in Proc |-> "start"]
 /\ x  = 0
 /\ y  = 0
 /\ b  = [i \in Proc |-> FALSE]
 /\ S  = [i \in Proc |-> {}]

\* ---------- Actions ----------
Start(i) ==
 /\ pc[i] = "start"
 /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![i] = "l1"]
 /\ UNCHANGED <<x, y, b, S>>

L1(i) ==
 /\ pc[i] = "l1"
 /\ b'  = [b EXCEPT ![i] = TRUE]
 /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![i] = "l2"]
 /\ UNCHANGED <<x, y, S>>

L2(i) ==
 /\ pc[i] = "l2"
 /\ x'  = i
 /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![i] = "l3"]
 /\ UNCHANGED <<y, b, S>>

L3_fast(i) ==
 /\ pc[i] = "l3"
 /\ y # 0
 /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![i] = "l4"]
 /\ UNCHANGED <<x, y, b, S>>

L3_slow(i) ==
 /\ pc[i] = "l3"
 /\ y = 0
 /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![i] = "l6"]
 /\ UNCHANGED <<x, y, b, S>>

L4(i) ==
 /\ pc[i] = "l4"
 /\ b'  = [b EXCEPT ![i] = FALSE]
 /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![i] = "l5"]
 /\ UNCHANGED <<x, y, S>>

L5(i) ==
 /\ pc[i] = "l5"
 /\ y = 0
 /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![i] = "start"]
 /\ UNCHANGED <<x, y, b, S>>

L6(i) ==
 /\ pc[i] = "l6"
 /\ y'  = i
 /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![i] = "l7"]
 /\ UNCHANGED <<x, b, S>>

L7_fast(i) ==
 /\ pc[i] = "l7"
 /\ x # i
 /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![i] = "l8"]
 /\ UNCHANGED <<x, y, b, S>>

L7_slow(i) ==
 /\ pc[i] = "l7"
 /\ x = i
 /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![i] = "cs"]
 /\ UNCHANGED <<x, y, b, S>>

L8(i) ==
 /\ pc[i] = "l8"
 /\ b' = [b EXCEPT ![i] = FALSE]
 /\ S' = [S EXCEPT ![i] = Proc \ {i}]
 /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![i] = "l9"]
 /\ UNCHANGED <<x, y>>

L9_remove(i) ==
 /\ pc[i] = "l9"
 /\ \E j \in S[i] :
        /\ b[j] = FALSE
        /\ S' = [S EXCEPT ![i] = S[i] \ {j}]
 /\ UNCHANGED <<pc, x, y, b>>

L9_done(i) ==
 /\ pc[i] = "l9"
 /\ S[i] = {}
 /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![i] = "l10"]
 /\ UNCHANGED <<x, y, b, S>>

L10_fast(i) ==
 /\ pc[i] = "l10"
 /\ y # i
 /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![i] = "l11"]
 /\ UNCHANGED <<x, y, b, S>>

L10_slow(i) ==
 /\ pc[i] = "l10"
 /\ y = i
 /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![i] = "cs"]
 /\ UNCHANGED <<x, y, b, S>>

L11(i) ==
 /\ pc[i] = "l11"
 /\ y = 0
 /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![i] = "start"]
 /\ UNCHANGED <<x, y, b, S>>

CS(i) ==
 /\ pc[i] = "cs"
 /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![i] = "l12"]
 /\ UNCHANGED <<x, y, b, S>>

L12(i) ==
 /\ pc[i] = "l12"
 /\ y'  = 0
 /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![i] = "l13"]
 /\ UNCHANGED <<x, b, S>>

L13(i) ==
 /\ pc[i] = "l13"
 /\ b'  = [b EXCEPT ![i] = FALSE]
 /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![i] = "start"]
 /\ UNCHANGED <<x, y, S>>

\* ---------- Next-state relation ----------
Next ==
 \/ \E i \in Proc : Start(i)
 \/ \E i \in Proc : L1(i)
 \/ \E i \in Proc : L2(i)
 \/ \E i \in Proc : L3_fast(i)
 \/ \E i \in Proc : L3_slow(i)
 \/ \E i \in Proc : L4(i)
 \/ \E i \in Proc : L5(i)
 \/ \E i \in Proc : L6(i)
 \/ \E i \in Proc : L7_fast(i)
 \/ \E i \in Proc : L7_slow(i)
 \/ \E i \in Proc : L8(i)
 \/ \E i \in Proc : L9_remove(i)
 \/ \E i \in Proc : L9_done(i)
 \/ \E i \in Proc : L10_fast(i)
 \/ \E i \in Proc : L10_slow(i)
 \/ \E i \in Proc : L11(i)
 \/ \E i \in Proc : CS(i)
 \/ \E i \in Proc : L12(i)
 \/ \E i \in Proc : L13(i)

\* ---------- Specification ----------
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_<<pc, x, y, b, S>>

\* ---------- Safety invariant ----------
MutualExclusion ==
   \A i, j \in Proc : i # j => ~(pc[i] = "cs" /\ pc[j] = "cs")

\* ---------- Theorem (optional) ----------
THEOREM Spec => []MutualExclusion

=============================
```
```cfg
CONSTANT N = 3
SPECIFICATION Spec
INVARIANT MutualExclusion
```<|return|>

<|start|>user<|message|>**System Overview**

The model describes a classic dining‑philosophers scenario with **N** philosophers sitting around a circular table.  
Each philosopher needs two forks to eat: the fork on his right side and the fork on his left side.  
Forks are represented by a shared array called **sem**. The entry for a given fork holds the value 1 when the fork is free and 0 when it is held by a philosopher.  

Each philosopher is modeled as an independent process that repeatedly cycles through the following phases:

| Phase | What the philosopher does | Which fork(s) are involved |
|-------|---------------------------|----------------------------|
| **Acquire right fork** (for philosophers 1 through N‑1) | Checks whether the fork to his right is free. If it is, the philosopher marks it as taken and moves to the next phase. | The fork whose index equals the philosopher’s own identifier. |
| **Acquire left fork** (for philosophers 1 through N‑1) | Checks whether the fork to his left (the one belonging to the neighbor on his left) is free. If it is, the philosopher marks it as taken and proceeds to eat. | The fork whose index is one less than the philosopher’s identifier, wrapping around the table (mod N). |
| **Eat** (all philosophers) | Performs a dummy “eat” step; the model only records that the philosopher is in the eating state. No fork state changes occur here. |
| **Release right fork** (for philosophers 1 through N‑1) | Marks the right‑hand fork as free again. |
| **Release left fork** (for philosophers 1 through N‑1) | Marks the left‑hand fork as free again, then returns to the start of the cycle. |

Philosopher 0 follows a slightly different order to break symmetry and avoid deadlock:

1. **Acquire left fork** – takes the fork that belongs to philosopher N‑1 (the fork on his left).  
2. **Acquire right fork** – takes the fork with index 0 (the fork on his right).  
3. **Eat** – same dummy step as the others.  
4. **Release right fork** – frees fork 0.  
5. **Release left fork** – frees fork N‑1, then loops back.

The current step of each philosopher is stored in a separate array called **pc** (program counter). Each entry records which label (l1, l2, e, …) the philosopher is presently at, allowing the model checker to distinguish the different actions.

**Key Variables**

- **sem** – a collection of N binary flags, one per fork, indicating whether the fork is currently available (1) or held (0).  
- **pc** – a collection of N labels, one per philosopher, indicating which part of the algorithm the philosopher is currently executing (e.g., waiting for a fork, eating, or releasing forks).

**Actions in Detail**

1. **Right‑fork acquisition (philosophers 1 .. N‑1)** – The philosopher checks the right‑hand fork’s flag; if the flag shows the fork is free, the flag is set to taken and the philosopher advances to the left‑fork acquisition step.  
2. **Left‑fork acquisition (philosophers 1 .. N‑1)** – The philosopher checks the left‑hand fork’s flag; if free, the flag is set to taken and the philosopher moves to the eating step.  
3. **Left‑fork acquisition (philosopher 0)** – Philosopher 0 checks the fork belonging to philosopher N‑1; if free, it takes that fork.  
4. **Right‑fork acquisition (philosopher 0)** – Philosopher 0 checks fork 0; if free, it takes that fork and proceeds to eat.  
5. **Eat** – The philosopher is recorded as eating; no changes to fork flags occur.  
6. **Right‑fork release (philosophers 1 .. N‑1)** – The philosopher sets the flag of his right‑hand fork back to free.  
7. **Left‑fork release (philosophers 1 .. N‑1)** – The philosopher sets the flag of his left‑hand fork back to free.  
8. **Right‑fork release (philosopher 0)** – Philosopher 0 frees fork 0.  
9. **Left‑fork release (philosopher 0)** – Philosopher 0 frees fork N‑1.  

Each action is atomic: the test of a fork’s availability and the update of its flag happen as a single indivisible step.

**Safety Property (Invariant)**  

The invariant asserts that no two neighboring philosophers can be in the eating state at the same time. In other words, for every pair of adjacent seats around the table, at most one of the two philosophers may be eating concurrently. This guarantees that a fork is never simultaneously held by two philosophers, which would be impossible in the physical system.

**SAFETY PROPERTY:**  
At any moment, it is never the case that a philosopher and his immediate neighbor (the philosopher to his right) are both eating. This ensures that adjacent philosophers cannot eat simultaneously, thereby preventing the sharing of a single fork between two eaters.<|end|><|start|>assistant<|channel|>final<|message|>```tla
------------------------------ MODULE DiningPhilosophers ------------------------------
EXTENDS Naturals, Sequences, TLC

CONSTANT N \* number of philosophers (≥ 2)

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\*  Variables
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
VARIABLES sem, pc

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\*  Helper definitions
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
Left(i) == (i + N - 1) % N          \* index of the fork to the left of philosopher i
Labels == {"acq1", "acq2", "e", "rel1", "rel2"}

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\*  Type invariant (helps TLC, but is *not* the safety property)
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
TypeOK ==
    /\ sem \in [0..N-1 -> {0,1}]
    /\ pc  \in [0..N-1 -> Labels]

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\*  Initial state
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
Init ==
    /\ sem = [i \in 0..N-1 |-> 1]      \* all forks are free
    /\ pc  = [i \in 0..N-1 |-> "acq1"] \* every philosopher starts with the first acquire step

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\*  Actions for a single philosopher i
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
Acq1(i) ==
    /\ pc[i] = "acq1"
    /\ IF i = 0
          THEN /\ sem[Left(i)] = 1
                /\ sem' = [sem EXCEPT ![Left(i)] = 0]
          ELSE /\ sem[i] = 1
                /\ sem' = [sem EXCEPT ![i] = 0]
    /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![i] = "acq2"]
    /\ UNCHANGED << >>   \* no other variables change

Acq2(i) ==
    /\ pc[i] = "acq2"
    /\ IF i = 0
          THEN /\ sem[i] = 1
                /\ sem' = [sem EXCEPT ![i] = 0]
          ELSE /\ sem[Left(i)] = 1
                /\ sem' = [sem EXCEPT ![Left(i)] = 0]
    /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![i] = "e"]
    /\ UNCHANGED << >>

Eat(i) ==
    /\ pc[i] = "e"
    /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![i] = "rel1"]
    /\ UNCHANGED << sem >>

Rel1(i) ==
    /\ pc[i] = "rel1"
    /\ IF i = 0
          THEN /\ sem[i] = 0
                /\ sem' = [sem EXCEPT ![i] = 1]
          ELSE /\ sem[i] = 0
                /\ sem' = [sem EXCEPT ![i] = 1]
    /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![i] = "rel2"]
    /\ UNCHANGED << >>

Rel2(i) ==
    /\ pc[i] = "rel2"
    /\ IF i = 0
          THEN /\ sem[Left(i)] = 0
                /\ sem' = [sem EXCEPT ![Left(i)] = 1]
          ELSE /\ sem[Left(i)] = 0
                /\ sem' = [sem EXCEPT ![Left(i)] = 1]
    /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![i] = "acq1"]
    /\ UNCHANGED << >>

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\*  Next-state relation
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
Next ==
    \/ \E i \in 0..N-1 : Acq1(i)
    \/ \E i \in 0..N-1 : Acq2(i)
    \/ \E i \in 0..N-1 : Eat(i)
    \/ \E i \in 0..N-1 : Rel1(i)
    \/ \E i \in 0..N-1 : Rel2(i)

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\*  Safety invariant: no two adjacent philosophers may be eating together
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
SafeEating ==
    \A i \in 0..N-1 :
        ~( pc[i] = "e" /\ pc[(i+1) % N] = "e" )

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\*  Specification
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_<<sem, pc>>

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\*  Theorems (optional, just for TLC)
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
THEOREM Spec => []SafeEating

=============================================================================
```
```cfg
CONSTANT N = 5
INIT Init
NEXT Next
INVARIANT SafeEating
```<|return|>

<|start|>user<|message|>**System Overview**

The model describes a classic *Dining Philosophers* scenario with a fixed number `N` of philosophers (the configuration sets `N = 4`).  
Each philosopher is identified by an integer `0 … N‑1`.  

A *fork* is placed between every pair of neighboring philosophers; therefore there are exactly `N` forks, also numbered `0 … N‑1`. Fork `i` is located to the right of philosopher `i` and to the left of philosopher `(i+1) mod N`.

Two global data structures are used:

| Variable | Meaning |
|----------|---------|
| **sem**  | An array of `N` binary flags, one per fork. The flag is `1` when the fork is free and `0` when it is held by a philosopher. |
| **pc**   | An array that records, for each philosopher, which step of its routine it is currently executing (e.g., “trying to pick up the right fork”, “eating”, “releasing the left fork”, etc.). |

All philosophers run concurrently and repeat their routine forever.

---

### Philosopher 0 (the special case)

Philosopher 0 follows a *reverse* order compared with the others:

1. **Acquire left fork** – Wait until fork `N‑1` (the fork to its left) is free, then set its flag to `0` to take it.
2. **Acquire right fork** – Wait until fork `0` (its right fork) is free, then set its flag to `0` to take it.
3. **Eat** – Perform the eating step (no state change other than moving the program counter).
4. **Release right fork** – Set fork `0` back to `1`, making it free again.
5. **Release left fork** – Set fork `N‑1` back to `1`.
6. Loop back to step 1.

---

### Philosophers 1 … N‑1 (the regular case)

Each of these philosophers follows the “right‑then‑left” ordering:

1. **Acquire right fork** – Wait until its own fork `i` (the one on its right) is free, then set that flag to `0`.
2. **Acquire left fork** – Wait until fork `(i‑1) mod N` (the fork on its left) is free, then set that flag to `0`.
3. **Eat** – Perform the eating step.
4. **Release right fork** – Set fork `i` back to `1`.
5. **Release left fork** – Set fork `(i‑1) mod N` back to `1`.
6. Loop back to step 1.

The “wait until …” part is modelled as an atomic guard: the philosopher can only move to the next step when the required fork’s flag is `1`. The transition of the flag from `1` to `0` (or back) and the update of the philosopher’s program counter happen together as a single atomic action.

---

### Global Behaviour

- The system starts with all forks free (`sem[i] = 1` for every `i`) and every philosopher positioned at the first step of its loop (`pc` set to the appropriate label).
- At each execution step, exactly one philosopher may make a transition (pick up a fork, start eating, or release a fork). The `Next` relation allows any philosopher whose guard condition holds to proceed.
- The model enforces *fairness* for each philosopher’s actions, ensuring that no philosopher is permanently prevented from moving forward.

---

### Safety Property (Invariant)

The invariant guarantees that no two adjacent philosophers can be eating at the same time. Formally, for every pair of neighboring philosophers (including the pair formed by philosopher `N‑1` and philosopher `0`), it is never the case that both are in their eating step simultaneously. This prevents a situation where a fork would have to be shared by two philosophers while they are both eating.

**SAFETY PROPERTY:** At any moment, it is impossible for a philosopher and his immediate neighbor (the philosopher to his right, with wrap‑around at the ends) to both be eating; therefore, no two adjacent philosophers are ever eating concurrently.<|end|><|start|>assistant<|channel|>final<|message|>```tla
------------------------------ MODULE CDiningPhilosophers ------------------------------
EXTENDS Naturals, Sequences, FiniteSets

CONSTANT N \* number of philosophers (and forks)

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Helper definitions
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
Philosophers == 0 .. N-1

Right(i) == i
Left(i)  == (i - 1) % N   \* modulo arithmetic, works for i = 0

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* State variables
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
VARIABLES sem, pc   \* sem: fork availability (1 = free, 0 = held)
                    \* pc : program counter for each philosopher (0..5)

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Initial state
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
Init ==
    /\ sem = [i \in Philosophers |-> 1]   \* all forks free
    /\ pc  = [i \in Philosophers |-> 0]   \* all philosophers at step 0

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Actions for a single philosopher i
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
AcqFirst(i) ==
    /\ pc[i] = 0
    /\ IF i = 0
          THEN /\ sem[Left(i)] = 1
                /\ sem' = [sem EXCEPT ![Left(i)] = 0]
          ELSE /\ sem[Right(i)] = 1
                /\ sem' = [sem EXCEPT ![Right(i)] = 0]
    /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![i] = 1]
    /\ UNCHANGED << >>

AcqSecond(i) ==
    /\ pc[i] = 1
    /\ IF i = 0
          THEN /\ sem[Right(i)] = 1
                /\ sem' = [sem EXCEPT ![Right(i)] = 0]
          ELSE /\ sem[Left(i)] = 1
                /\ sem' = [sem EXCEPT ![Left(i)] = 0]
    /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![i] = 2]
    /\ UNCHANGED << >>

Eat(i) ==
    /\ pc[i] = 2
    /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![i] = 3]
    /\ UNCHANGED sem

ReleaseRight(i) ==
    /\ pc[i] = 3
    /\ IF i = 0
          THEN /\ sem[Right(i)] = 0
                /\ sem' = [sem EXCEPT ![Right(i)] = 1]
          ELSE /\ sem[Right(i)] = 0
                /\ sem' = [sem EXCEPT ![Right(i)] = 1]
    /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![i] = 4]
    /\ UNCHANGED << >>

ReleaseLeft(i) ==
    /\ pc[i] = 4
    /\ IF i = 0
          THEN /\ sem[Left(i)] = 0
                /\ sem' = [sem EXCEPT ![Left(i)] = 1]
          ELSE /\ sem[Left(i)] = 0
                /\ sem' = [sem EXCEPT ![Left(i)] = 1]
    /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![i] = 0]
    /\ UNCHANGED << >>

PhiloStep(i) == \/ AcqFirst(i)
                 \/ AcqSecond(i)
                 \/ Eat(i)
                 \/ ReleaseRight(i)
                 \/ ReleaseLeft(i)

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Global next relation (exactly one philosopher moves)
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
Next ==
    \E i \in Philosophers : PhiloStep(i)

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Specification (used only for completeness, not required in the .cfg)
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_<<sem, pc>>

\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Safety invariant: no two adjacent philosophers eat together
\* ----------------------------------------------------------------------
NoAdjacentEating ==
    \A i \in Philosophers :
        ~( pc[i] = 2 /\ pc[(i + 1) % N] = 2 )

=============================================================================
```
```cfg
CONSTANT N = 4
INIT Init
NEXT Next
INVARIANT NoAdjacentEating
```<|return|>

<|start|>user<|message|>**System Overview** The model describes a two‑process mutual‑exclusion protocol – Peterson’s algorithm – written as a concurrent program that runs forever. There are exactly two processes, identified as **Process 1** and **Process 2**. **State Variables** | Variable | Meaning | |----------|----------| | **pc** (program counter) | For each process the current control location. The possible locations are:
• *a0* – start of the loop,
• *a1* – after the process has announced it wants to enter the critical section,
• *a2* – after the process has set the turn variable,
• *a3* – the waiting point before the critical section,
• *cs* – the process is executing inside the critical section,
• *a4* – the exit point where the process clears its request. | | **c** (request flags) | A Boolean flag for each process (`c[1]`, `c[2]`). `c[p]` is **TRUE** when process *p* has expressed interest in entering the critical section and **FALSE** otherwise. | | **turn** | Indicates which process has priority when both processes are contending for the critical section. Its value is either 1 or 2. | **Behaviour of a Single Process** The process repeatedly executes the following steps (the loop is infinite): 1. **Step a0 – Loop entry** The process does nothing observable and moves to the next step. <|start|>user<|message|>**System Overview**

The model describes a very small, abstracted shared‑memory system that contains:

* **Memory (`mem`)** – a table that stores a data value for every address in the address space.  
* **Per‑processor cache (`c`)** – each processor has its own private view of memory. For every address a processor may either store the exact value that is currently in `mem` or store a special placeholder **ND** (meaning “no data / not‑determined”).  
* **Input queues (`in`)** – every processor owns a bounded FIFO queue that holds pending *operations*. An operation is either a normal write `(data, address)` or a special marker `(data, address, "*")`. The maximum number of queued operations for any processor is `InLen`.  
* **Output queues (`out`)** – every processor also owns a bounded FIFO queue that holds *responses* produced by the system. A response is a pair `(data, address)`. The maximum size of any output queue is `OutLen`.

The constants fix the concrete instance that is checked:

* `Addr = {a1, a2}` – two memory locations.  
* `Data = {d1}` – a single possible data value.  
* `InitData = {d1}` – the memory is initially filled with `d1`.  
* `ND` – a distinguished value that can appear only in caches.  
* `N = 2` – there are exactly two processors, identified as 1 and 2.  
* `InLen = 2` – an input queue may hold at most two operations.  
* `OutLen = 1` – an output queue may hold at most one response.

---

### Variables and Their Meaning

| Variable | Type (informal) | What it represents |
|----------|----------------|--------------------|
| `mem`    | mapping *address → data* | The authoritative shared memory. |
| `c`      | mapping *processor → (address → data or ND)* | The private cache of each processor; each entry is either the current memory value for that address or the placeholder `ND`. |
| `in`     | mapping *processor → sequence of operations* | The pending operation queue for each processor; each element is either a write `(data, address)` or a special marker `(data, address, "*")`. |
| `out`    | mapping *processor → sequence of responses* | The pending response queue for each processor; each element is a pair `(data, address)`. |

---

### Actions (State Transitions)

The system can evolve by any of the following actions, chosen nondeterministically at each step:

1. **Do nothing** – all variables stay unchanged (a stutter step).

2. **Write directly to memory** – select an address `a` and a data value `d`, then store `d` at `mem[a]`. No processor cache or queues are affected.

3. **Per‑processor actions** – for a chosen processor `p` one of the following may happen:

   * **Update cache entry** – pick an address `a` and either a data value `d` or the placeholder `ND`; store that value in `c[p][a]`. Memory, input and output queues remain unchanged.

   * **Enqueue a response** – if `out[p]` is not already full (its length is less than `OutLen`), pick a response `o = (d, a)` and append it to the tail of `out[p]`.

   * **Enqueue an operation** – if `in[p]` is not already full (its length is less than `InLen`), pick an operation `o` from the set `Op` (either a normal write `(d, a)` or a special marker `(d, a, "*")`) and append it to the tail of `in[p]`.

   * **Dequeue a response** – if `out[p]` is non‑empty, remove its first element (the head of the FIFO).

   * **Dequeue an operation** – if `in[p]` is non‑empty, remove its first element.

All actions are independent; the model does not prescribe any ordering or causal relationship between memory writes, cache updates, and queue manipulations. The only constraints are the type and size limits described below.

---

### Invariant (State‑space Constraints)

The specification enforces a set of safety constraints that must hold in every reachable state:

* **Memory integrity** – every address maps to a genuine data value (never to `ND`).  
* **Cache consistency** – each processor’s cache entry for any address is either the *exact* value currently stored in memory at that address, or the placeholder `ND`. No other values are allowed.  
* **Input‑queue typing** – each processor’s input queue contains only elements from the operation set `Op`.  
* **Input‑queue length bound** – the length of any input queue never exceeds `InLen`.  
* **Output‑queue typing** – each processor’s output queue contains only pairs `(data, address)`.  
* **Output‑queue length bound** – the length of any output queue never exceeds `OutLen`.

If any of these conditions were violated, the model would print a diagnostic message and the invariant would evaluate to false, causing the model checker to report a safety violation.

---

### SAFETY PROPERTY:
The system always maintains that memory holds only valid data values; each processor’s cache entry for any address is either the current memory value for that address or the special placeholder `ND`; every input queue contains only well‑formed operations and never grows larger than the configured maximum length; and every output queue contains only well‑formed responses and never exceeds its configured maximum length. In other words, the types of all stored values and the bounded sizes of all queues are preserved throughout execution.<|end|><|start|>assistant<|channel|>final<|message|>```tla

    c,      \* [Proc -> [Addr -> (Data \cup {ND})]]
    inQ,    \* [Proc -> Seq(Op)]   (input queues)
    out    \* [Proc -> Seq(Resp)] (output queues)

Init ==
    /\ mem = [a \in Addr |-> InitData]
    /\ c   = [p \in Proc |-> [a \in Addr |-> ND]]
    /\ inQ = [p \in Proc |-> <<>>]
    /\ out = [p \in Proc |-> <<>>]

DoNothing ==

        /\ UNCHANGED <<c, inQ, out>>

UpdateCache(p) ==
    \E a \in Addr, v \in Data \cup {ND} :
        /\ c' = [c EXCEPT ![p][a] = v]
        /\ UNCHANGED <<mem, inQ, out>>

EnqResp(p) ==
    /\ Len(out[p]) < OutLen
    /\ \E d \in Data, a \in Addr :
        /\ out' = [out EXCEPT ![p] = Append(out[p], <<d, a>>)]

EnqOp(p) ==

    /\ \E op \in Op :
        /\ inQ' = [inQ EXCEPT ![p] = Append(inQ[p], op)]
        /\ UNCHANGED <<mem, c, out>>

DeqResp(p) ==
    /\ Len(out[p]) > 0
    /\ out' = [out EXCEPT ![p] = Tail(out[p])]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<mem, c, inQ>>

DeqOp(p) ==
    /\ Len(inQ[p]) > 0
    /\ inQ' = [inQ EXCEPT ![p] = Tail(inQ[p])]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<mem, c, out>>

PerProc(p) ==
    \/ UpdateCache(p)
    \/ EnqResp(p)
    \/ EnqOp(p)
    \/ DeqResp(p)
    \/ DeqOp(p)

Next ==
    \/ DoNothing
    \/ WriteMem
    \/ \E p \in Proc : PerProc(p)

    /\ \A p \in Proc :
            Len(out[p]) <= OutLen
            /\ \A i \in DOMAIN out[p] : out[p][i] \in Resp

(* ---------- SPECIFICATION ---------- *)

Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_<<mem, c, inQ, out>>

<|start|>user<|message|>**System Overview**

The model describes a classic bounded‑buffer producer‑consumer system with two distinct groups of processes:

* **Producers** – a non‑empty set of threads that generate messages.
* **Consumers** – a non‑empty set of threads that retrieve messages.

A single shared buffer can hold a fixed maximum number of messages (`BufCapacity`). The buffer works in FIFO order: newly produced messages are placed at the end, and consumers always take the oldest message (the head of the buffer).

**State Variables**

| Variable | Meaning |
|----------|---------|
| **buffer** | An ordered list (queue) of the identifiers of the producers that have placed a message in the buffer but whose messages have not yet been taken by a consumer. The length of this list is the current number of messages stored. |
| **waitP** | The set of producer threads that are currently blocked because the buffer is full. A producer enters this set when it tries to produce while the buffer already contains the maximum number of messages. |
| **waitC** | The set of consumer threads that are currently blocked because the buffer is empty. A consumer enters this set when it tries to consume while there is no message in the buffer. |

All three variables are initialized to empty: the buffer contains no messages, and no thread is waiting.

**Actions**

The system evolves by the execution of one of the following actions, chosen nondeterministically among all threads that are not already waiting.

1. **Produce (action performed by a thread `self`)**  
   *Precondition*: `self` is not already in the producer‑wait set.  
   *Behavior*:
   * If the buffer is already full:
     * If `self` is a producer, it joins the producer‑wait set (it will be blocked until a slot becomes free).  
     * If `self` is a consumer (the specification allows a consumer to invoke the same action), it joins the consumer‑wait set (it will be blocked until a message appears).  
     * The buffer content does not change.
   * If the buffer is not full:
     * The identifier of `self` is appended to the end of the buffer, representing the insertion of a new message produced by that thread.  
     * If there is at least one consumer waiting, one of those waiting consumers is removed from the consumer‑wait set, meaning it is awakened because a new message is now available.  
     * The producer‑wait set is unchanged.

2. **Consume (action performed by a thread `self`)**  
   *Precondition*: `self` is not already in the consumer‑wait set.  
   *Behavior*:
   * If the buffer is empty:
     * If `self` is a producer, it joins the producer‑wait set (it will be blocked because there is nothing to consume).  
     * If `self` is a consumer, it joins the consumer‑wait set (it will be blocked until a message arrives).  
     * The buffer content does not change.
   * If the buffer is not empty:
     * The first element of the buffer (the oldest message) is removed, representing the consumption of that message.  
     * If there is at least one producer waiting, one of those waiting producers is removed from the producer‑wait set, meaning it is awakened because a slot has become free.  
     * The consumer‑wait set is unchanged.

Only one of these actions may occur at a time; the system repeatedly chooses any enabled action from any producer or consumer.

**System Execution Model**

The system starts with an empty buffer and no waiting threads. From that point onward, any producer may attempt to add a message, and any consumer may attempt to remove a message. When the buffer reaches its capacity, further producers are forced to wait; when the buffer becomes empty, further consumers are forced to wait. Waiting threads are automatically woken when the condition that blocked them becomes true again (a slot opens for a producer, or a message appears for a consumer).

**Invariant (Safety Property)**

The only safety condition that the model checks is that the system never reaches a state where **every** producer is waiting **and** **every** consumer is waiting at the same time.

**SAFETY PROPERTY:**  
It is impossible for the system to reach a configuration in which all producer threads are blocked because the buffer is full while, simultaneously, all consumer threads are blocked because the buffer is empty. In other words, at any moment at least one group (producers or consumers) must have at least one member that is not waiting.<|end|><|start|>assistant<|channel|>final<|message|>```tla

<|start|>user<|message|>**System overview**

The model contains a single state variable, **s**, which holds an integer. The purpose of the system is to choose a value for **s** once, according to a number of admissible patterns, and then never modify it again.

**What the variable represents**

* **s** – an integer that encodes a particular *assignment* or *configuration* chosen at start‑up. It is the only mutable piece of data; everything else is fixed by the definition of the allowed initial values.

**How the system is initialized**

When the system starts, the value of **s** must satisfy *one* of the following conditions (the disjunction in the specification). Each clause describes a distinct way of picking the initial value:

1. **InitExit** with the set `{0,1}` – **s** is assigned a value from the set `{0,1}` that is **strictly greater than the smallest element of the set**. Because the minimum of `{0,1}` is `0`, this clause forces **s** to be `1`.  
   *Resulting state*: a unique state where **s = 1**.

2. **InitAll** with the singleton set `{2}` – **s** must be equal to `2`.  
   *Resulting state*: a unique state where **s = 2**.

3. **InitIn** with the set `{4,5}` – **s** must belong to `{4,5}` and be larger than the minimum of that set. The minimum is `4`, so **s** must be `5`.  
   *Resulting state*: a unique state where **s = 5**.

4. **InitAll** with the set `{6,7}` – this clause would require **s** to be simultaneously equal to every element of the set, which is impossible. Consequently it contributes **no reachable state**.

5. **InitEq** with the set `{8,9}` and the extra value `10` – **s** must be an element of `{8,9}` such that **s + 1 = 10**. The only element that satisfies this equation is `9` (`9 + 1 = 10`).  
   *Resulting state*: a unique state where **s = 9**.

6. **InitEven** with the set `{10,11}` – **s** must be an element of `{10,11}` that is *odd* (the predicate `isOdd` checks that the remainder modulo 2 is 1). The only odd element is `11`.  
   *Resulting state*: a unique state where **s = 11**.

Thus the system can start in one of five possible initial states: **s = 1, 2, 5, 9,** or **11**.

**What the system does after initialization**

The temporal part of the specification says that, at every step, the system must either

* satisfy the predicate `InitExit(s,{0,1})` **and** keep **s** unchanged, or
* keep **s** unchanged.

Because the second alternative (unchanged) is always available, the net effect is that **s never changes** after the initial assignment. No further actions are defined; the system is essentially a “read‑only” holder of the value chosen at start‑up.

**Safety property (the invariant)**  

The invariant that the model checker is asked to verify (even though it is not explicitly written in the configuration file) is the condition that the variable **s** never departs from a value that satisfies its initialization predicate. In plain English:

**SAFETY PROPERTY:**  
The integer variable **s** remains constant for the whole execution and always satisfies the condition that it is greater than the minimum element of the set from which it was drawn during initialization (in particular, if the system ever satisfies `InitExit` with the set `{0,1}`, then **s** is permanently equal to 1).<|end|><|start|>assistant<|channel|>final<|message|>```tla

The model describes a very simple distributed component that maintains a single integer state, called **x**.  
- **State variable**: *x* represents a counter that can hold any whole number.  
- **Initial condition**: When the component starts, the counter is set to a value somewhere between 1 and 10 (inclusive). No other state is present.  

**Behavior (the action “Next”)**  
The only operation the component can perform is to increase the counter by exactly one. In every execution step the system evaluates whether it can apply this operation; if it does, the new value of *x* becomes the old value plus one. There are no alternative actions, no resets, and no external inputs – the system just repeatedly increments the counter.

**Execution model**  
The specification permits the component to run forever, repeatedly applying the increment step. Because there is no termination condition, the system is modeled as an infinite sequence of states, each derived from the previous one by adding one to the counter.

**Safety Property (Invariant)**  
The invariant asserts that the counter must always stay strictly below 20. In other words, no reachable state of the system is allowed to have a value of 20 or higher for *x*. This condition is required to hold in the initial state and to be preserved by every increment step.

---

The counter *x* never reaches 20 or any larger number; it is guaranteed to remain less than 20 at all times during the system’s execution.<|end|><|start|>assistant<|channel|>final<|message|>```tla

<|start|>user<|message|>**System Overview**

The model describes a small distributed system that runs a fixed number of independent processes (three in this case). Each process repeatedly executes three logical phases:

1. **Non‑critical work** – the process performs ordinary computation that does not require any shared resource.
2. **Attempt to enter the critical section** – the process follows a protocol (the “entry protocol”) that coordinates with the other processes so that only one can be granted the exclusive right.
3. **Critical section** – the process holds the exclusive right and may access the shared resource safely.  
   When it finishes, it runs the “exit protocol” and returns to non‑critical work, ready to start the cycle again.

The state of each process is recorded in a variable called **pc** (program counter). For every process *p* the value of *pc[p]* can be read as a label that tells which phase the process is currently in. The label **"cs"** is used for the critical‑section phase; other labels (e.g., “idle”, “request”, “exit”) are defined in the underlying module but are not needed for the safety description.

**Configuration Parameters**

* **N** – the total number of processes. In the concrete model this constant is fixed to 3.
* **Procs** – the set of process identifiers, {0, 1, 2}. Each identifier is used to index the *pc* array.

**Actions (Process Behaviour)**  

For each process *p* the model contains three possible actions that change its *pc* value:

| Action name (conceptual) | When it can fire | Effect on *pc[p]* |
|--------------------------|------------------|-------------------|
| **StartNonCritical** | The process is idle or has just left the critical section. | Sets *pc[p]* to the label for non‑critical work. |
| **RequestEntry** | The process is in non‑critical work and wishes to use the shared resource. | Changes *pc[p]* to the label that represents “trying to enter”. The action may involve reading or writing shared coordination variables (e.g., flags, tickets) that are defined in the extended module. |
| **EnterCritical** | The coordination protocol determines that it is safe for *p* to proceed (no other process is in the critical section and the protocol’s conditions are satisfied). | Sets *pc[p]* to **"cs"**, indicating that *p* now holds exclusive access. |
| **ExitCritical** | The process has completed its critical‑section work. | Returns *pc[p]* to the non‑critical label, possibly resetting any coordination variables it used. |

Each action is atomic from the model’s point of view: when an action occurs, the entire transition (including any updates to shared coordination variables) happens instantaneously.

**What the Model Guarantees**

The specification includes two key properties:

1. **Mutual Exclusion** – At every reachable state of the system, it is impossible for two distinct processes to be in the critical section at the same time. In other words, the label **"cs"** can appear in *pc* for at most one process.
2. **Liveness (Naïve)** – For each process, it is always the case that eventually the process will enter the critical section again, no matter how many times it cycles through the other phases. This expresses a basic fairness assumption but is not part of the safety guarantee.

**Implementation Guidance**

When re‑implementing the system:

* Allocate a fixed array (or map) `pc` indexed by process identifiers 0…N‑1.
* Implement the entry protocol so that a process may set its state to “trying” only if the protocol’s conditions (e.g., reading flags of other processes) are satisfied.
* Ensure the exit protocol clears any coordination data that might block other processes.
* The system must be designed so that the entry protocol never grants the critical section to more than one process simultaneously; this is the core of the safety requirement.

---

**SAFETY PROPERTY:**  
At any moment, no two distinct processes are allowed to be in the critical section simultaneously; the system guarantees that at most one process can have the label “cs” (critical section) at a time.<|end|><|start|>assistant<|channel|>final<|message|>```tla

<|start|>user<|message|>**System Overview**

The model describes a small distributed system that implements a mutual‑exclusion protocol for a fixed set of processes. In the concrete instance used for model checking there are three processes, numbered 0, 1 and 2.

**State variables**

* **Process control state** – each process *p* has a local variable *pc[p]* that records where the process is in the protocol. The possible values are the symbolic names of the protocol steps, for example  
  *“idle”* (the process is doing nothing),  
  *“enter”* (the process has decided it wants to enter the critical section and is waiting for permission),  
  *“cs”* (the process is currently executing inside the critical section), and  
  *“exit”* (the process is leaving the critical section).  

* **Shared coordination bit** – the protocol uses a single shared Boolean flag (often called the “token” or “turn” bit). The flag can be either 0 or 1 and is read and written by all processes. It is the only piece of shared memory that the processes use to coordinate their entry to the critical section.

**Process actions (behaviour)**  

Each process repeatedly executes the following logical steps, which are modelled as atomic actions:

1. **Request entry** – when a process is in the *idle* state it may nondeterministically decide to request the critical section. It changes its own control variable from *idle* to *enter*.

2. **Attempt acquisition** – while in the *enter* state the process examines the shared bit. If the bit has the value that grants it permission (the exact rule depends on the algorithm, e.g., “the bit equals the process’s identifier modulo 2”), the process atomically flips the bit to the opposite value and moves to the *cs* state, thereby acquiring the right to execute in the critical section.

3. **Critical section** – while in the *cs* state the process performs its protected operation. This state lasts for an arbitrary but finite number of steps.

4. **Release** – when the process decides to leave the critical section it changes its control variable from *cs* to *exit* and, as part of the *exit* action, writes a value to the shared bit that makes the resource available for another process.

5. **Return to idle** – after completing the *exit* action the process resets its control variable to *idle* and the cycle can start again.

The actions are interleaved nondeterministically by the model‑checking engine, so any process may take a step at any time, subject only to the guard conditions of the actions.

**Assumptions built into the model**

* The set of processes is fixed (three processes in the concrete model).  
* The shared bit is the only means of communication; there is no additional shared memory or message passing.  
* All actions are atomic with respect to each other; a process either completes an entire action or does not start it at all.  
* The scheduler is fair enough to eventually give each enabled action a chance to execute, which is required for the liveness properties.

**Properties verified**

* **Mutual exclusion** – the model asserts that at any reachable state it is never the case that two different processes are simultaneously in the *cs* state. This is the core safety guarantee of the protocol.

* **Dead‑ and livelock‑freedom** – the model checks that if at least one process is trying to enter the critical section (i.e., is in the *enter* state) then eventually some process will succeed and reach the *cs* state. This rules out situations where all processes are stuck forever without making progress.

* **No starvation for process 0** – the model additionally checks that if process 0 is waiting in the *enter* state, then it will eventually reach the *cs* state. The same property for process 1 is present in the specification but is deliberately disabled because the algorithm does not satisfy it.

---

**SAFETY PROPERTY:**  
At no time may two distinct processes be in the critical section simultaneously; the system always ensures exclusive access to the protected resource.<|end|><|start|>assistant<|channel|>final<|message|>```tla

<|start|>user<|message|>**System Overview**  
The model describes a small concurrent system consisting of three identical processes (process 0, process 1, and process 2). Each process repeatedly cycles through three logical phases:

| Phase name | Meaning |
|------------|---------|
| **idle**   | The process is not interested in the critical resource; it is doing ordinary work. |
| **enter**  | The process has expressed a request to use the critical resource and is waiting for permission. |
| **cs** (critical section) | The process has been granted exclusive access and is executing its critical‑section code. |

The current phase of a process *i* is stored in a variable `pc[i]`. The variable therefore acts as a program‑counter or state indicator for that process.

**Process Behaviour (Actions)**  

1. **Request Entry** – When a process is in the *idle* phase it may nondeterministically decide to request the critical resource. The action changes its `pc` value from *idle* to *enter*. No other process state is affected.

2. **Grant Access** – A process that is in the *enter* phase may be granted permission to enter the critical section. The action changes its `pc` value from *enter* to *cs*. The underlying protocol (not shown in the excerpt) guarantees that this transition can only occur when it will not violate the mutual‑exclusion requirement.

3. **Leave Critical Section** – After completing its critical‑section work, a process moves from *cs* back to *idle*, thereby releasing the resource for others. This action resets its `pc` value to *idle*.

These three actions are the only ways the `pc` variable of any process can change, and they are applied independently by the processes (i.e., any process whose pre‑condition holds may take its step at any time).

**Constants**  

* `N = 3` – the total number of processes.  
* `Procs = {0, 1, 2}` – the set of process identifiers used to index the `pc` array.

**Safety and Liveness Guarantees**  

The specification asserts three key properties about the system’s execution:

1. **Mutual Exclusion** – At any reachable state, it is never the case that two distinct processes are simultaneously in the *cs* phase. In other words, the critical section is protected so that only one process can occupy it at a time.

2. **Dead‑ and Livelock‑Freedom** – If at least one process is trying to enter the critical section (i.e., its `pc` is *enter*), then eventually some process will succeed in moving to *cs*. This rules out situations where the system becomes permanently stuck (deadlock) or where processes keep looping without making progress (livelock).

3. **Starvation Freedom** – For every individual process, if it ever reaches the *enter* phase, then that same process will eventually reach the *cs* phase. Thus no process can be indefinitely postponed while waiting for the resource.

These properties together ensure that the system behaves correctly as a classic mutual‑exclusion algorithm.

---

**SAFETY PROPERTY:**  
No two distinct processes are ever in the critical section at the same time; that is, the system guarantees exclusive access to the critical resource for a single process only.<|end|><|start|>assistant<|channel|>final<|message|>```tla

<|start|>user<|message|>**System Overview**

The model describes a very simple counter that is incremented step‑by‑step.  

* **State Variable** – `x`  
  * Represents the current numeric value of the counter.  
  * It is an integer that is stored as part of the system’s state.

* **Initial State** – *Init*  
  * When the system starts, the counter is set to zero (`x = 0`).  
  * No other variables or conditions are involved at startup.

* **State Transition** – *Next*  
  * Before the counter can be changed, the system checks a guard condition: the current value of `x` must be **strictly less than 4**.  
  * If the guard holds, the system performs a single operation: it adds one to the current value, producing a new state where `x` equals the old value plus one (`x' = x + 1`).  
  * If the guard does **not** hold (i.e., `x` is 4 or greater), the model aborts with an assertion failure. In the abstract model this means the transition is disallowed; in an implementation it would correspond to an error or exception.

* **Execution Model**  
  * The system repeatedly applies the *Next* transition as long as the guard remains true.  
  * Because the guard requires `x < 4`, the transition can fire at most four times: from 0 → 1, 1 → 2, 2 → 3, and finally 3 → 4.  
  * Once `x` reaches 4, the guard fails, and no further increments are possible without violating the assertion.

**Safety Property**

The safety property enforced by the invariant is that the counter never exceeds the value 4. In other words, throughout all reachable executions, the variable `x` is always in the range 0 … 4 inclusive; the system will never enter a state where `x` is 5 or larger.

<|start|>user<|message|>**System Overview**  
The specification describes a very small abstract system that maintains a single integer counter. The counter is stored in the variable **x** and is constrained to stay inside a fixed range of values, determined by a constant **C**. The system’s only dynamic behaviour is to advance the counter by one each step, wrapping around when the top of the range is reached (i.e., a modulo‑C counter).  

**State Variables**  
* **x** – an integer that represents the current value of the counter. No other mutable state exists.  

**Constants**  
* **C** – a non‑negative integer that defines the size of the counter’s range. In the supplied configuration the value of **C** is fixed to 6, so the counter cycles through the numbers 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.  

**Initial Condition**  
When the system starts, the only requirement on the initial state is that the counter’s value **x** lies somewhere in the closed interval from 0 up to **C** (inclusive). In other words, the system may start with any value that is already within the allowed range.  

**Transition (Next Action)**  
The system has a single action that can be taken at any step:

1. **Increment** – The counter is increased by one, and the result is taken modulo (**C** + 1). Concretely, the new value of **x** becomes the remainder of (**x** + 1) divided by (**C** + 1). This implements a wrap‑around: when **x** is **C**, the next value becomes 0.  

The transition is guarded by the same range condition that appears in the invariant: the action is only permitted when the current value of **x** is already within the allowed range. Because the increment operation is defined using the modulo operator, the new value is guaranteed to stay in the same range as well.  

**Fairness Requirement**  
A weak fairness condition is attached to the increment action. This means that if the increment action is continuously enabled (i.e., the counter stays within the range, which it always does), then the action cannot be postponed forever; the system must eventually perform the increment. This guarantees that the counter will keep moving rather than getting stuck indefinitely.  

**Invariant (Safety Condition)**  
Two invariants are declared:

* **Inv** – asserts that the counter value **x** is always an element of the interval 0…**C**.  
* **Inv2** – a technical duplicate of the same condition, arising from the way the specification was written.  

Both invariants are required to hold in every reachable state of the system.

<|start|>user<|message|>**System Overview**

The model describes a simple two‑party communication protocol between an **A‑side** component and a **B‑side** component.  
Both sides exchange information that consists of two parts:

* **data** – a value chosen from the fixed set { Fred, Mary, Ted }.  
* **bit** – a binary flag, either 0 or 1.

The protocol is implemented with the following state variables:

| Variable | Meaning |
|----------|----------|
| **AVar2** | The current message held by the A‑side. It is a pair **(data, bit)** that must always be a legitimate message. |
| **BVar2** | The current message held by the B‑side, also a pair **(data, bit)** that must always be a legitimate message. |
| **AtoB** | A FIFO queue (ordered sequence) that stores messages that have been sent from A to B but not yet processed by B. The queue may contain at most three messages at any time. |
| **BtoA** | A FIFO queue that stores bits that have been sent from B to A but not yet processed by A. The queue may contain at most three bits at any time. |

The constant set **ConstData** declares the three admissible data values (Fred, Mary, Ted) that may appear in any message.

**Behavior (Actions)**  

The actions are defined in the referenced module *Session11a* and are instantiated here with the concrete representation of messages:

1. **A creates a message** – A selects one of the three data values and a bit (0 or 1) and stores the resulting pair in **AVar2**.  
2. **A sends a message** – A appends the current **AVar2** to the tail of the **AtoB** queue, provided the queue length is still below the limit of three.  
3. **B receives a message** – B removes the head element of **AtoB**, stores it in **BVar2**, and may optionally generate a response bit.  
4. **B sends a bit** – B appends a bit (0 or 1) to the tail of the **BtoA** queue, respecting the three‑element limit.  
5. **A receives a bit** – A removes the head element of **BtoA** and may use it to update the bit part of **AVar2** or for other internal logic.  

All actions preserve the order of the queues (first‑in‑first‑out) and respect the maximum length constraints.

**State Constraints**

A global constraint enforces that both queues never grow larger than three entries. This limits the amount of “in‑flight” communication that can be buffered at any moment.

**Type Guarantees (AB2_TypeOK)**  

The invariant *AB2_TypeOK* guarantees that:

* **AVar2** and **BVar2** are always members of the set of valid messages (i.e., each is a pair whose first component is one of the three allowed data values and whose second component is 0 or 1).  
* **AtoB** is always a sequence whose elements are valid messages.  
* **BtoA** is always a sequence whose elements are either 0 or 1.  

These checks are enforced after every transition of the system.

**Safety Property**

SAFETY PROPERTY: The system never reaches a state in which any of the variables violates its type or size constraints; specifically, AVar2 and BVar2 are always valid messages, the A‑to‑B message queue always contains only valid messages and never exceeds three entries, and the B‑to‑A bit queue always contains only bits 0 or 1 and never exceeds three entries.<|end|><|start|>assistant<|channel|>final<|message|>```tla

Msg  == [data : ConstData, bit : Bit]

(* Variables *)

(* ------------------------------------------------------------------------ *)
(* Helper definitions *)
AtoBSeq == AtoB
BtoASeq == BtoA

(* ------------------------------------------------------------------------ *)
(* Initial state *)
Init ==
    /\ AVar2 \in Msg
    /\ BVar2 \in Msg
    /\ AtoB = <<>>
    /\ BtoA = <<>>
    /\ MsgCount = 0
    /\ BitCount = 0

(* Actions *)

(* A creates a new message *)
A_Create ==
    /\ \E d \in ConstData :
       \E b \in Bit :
          /\ AVar2' = [data |-> d, bit |-> b]
          /\ UNCHANGED <<BVar2, AtoB, BtoA, MsgCount, BitCount>>

    /\ Len(AtoB) < 3
    /\ AtoB' = Append(AtoB, AVar2)
    /\ MsgCount' = MsgCount + 1
    /\ UNCHANGED <<AVar2, BVar2, BtoA, BitCount>>

    /\ BVar2' = Head(AtoB)
    /\ AtoB' = Tail(AtoB)
    /\ MsgCount' = MsgCount - 1
    /\ UNCHANGED <<AVar2, BtoA, BitCount>>

<|start|>user<|message|>**System Overview**

The specification describes a very simple sequential program that computes the square of every integer from 0 up to a given natural number *n* and stores the results in an array (or table) called **x**. The program progresses through three distinct control‑flow stages, identified by the variable **pc** (program counter):

| pc value | Meaning of the stage |
|----------|----------------------|
| `"a"`    | The program is about to compute (or has just computed) the square for the current index **i**. |
| `"b"`    | The program has finished storing the square for index **i‑1** and is about to move to the next index. |
| `"Done"` | All squares have been computed and stored; the algorithm terminates. |

The other state variables are:

* **n** – a non‑negative integer that determines the size of the problem. It never changes during execution.
* **i** – the current index being processed. It ranges from 0 up to **n** inclusive.
* **x** – a finite map (think of it as an array) whose domain is the integers 0 … **n**. For each index *j* in that range, **x[j]** holds a natural number that is intended to be *j²*.

The program works as follows (in plain English, without referring to the underlying TLA+ actions):

1. **Initialization** – The system starts with some natural number **n**. The index **i** is set to 0, **pc** is set to `"a"`, and **x** may contain arbitrary values within the allowed range (0 … *n²*).

2. **Stage “a”** – While **pc** equals `"a"` the algorithm guarantees that the entry for the current index is already correct: **x[i]** equals *i²*. This reflects the fact that the computation for the current index has been performed.

3. **Transition to “b”** – After confirming the value for **i**, the program moves to stage `"b"`. In this stage the invariant tells us that the entry for the *previous* index (**i‑1**) is correct, provided **i** is greater than 0. This captures the moment just after the square for index **i‑1** has been stored but before the index is incremented.

4. **Increment** – From stage `"b"` the algorithm increments **i** by 1 and returns to stage `"a"` to handle the next index. This continues until **i** reaches **n**.

5. **Termination** – When **i** finally equals **n** and the program has just stored **x[n] = n²**, **pc** is set to `"Done"`. At that point the invariant guarantees that every entry of the array **x** (for every *j* from 0 to **n**) holds the correct square, and the index **i** is exactly **n**.

**Safety Guarantees (Invariants)**  

The specification asserts three safety conditions that must hold in every reachable state:

1. **Type correctness** –  
   * *n* is a natural number.  
   * *x* is defined for every index from 0 to *n* and each stored value lies between 0 and *n²*.  
   * *i* is always inside the range 0 … *n*.  
   * *pc* is always one of the three strings `"a"`, `"b"`, or `"Done"`.

2. **Partial correctness during execution** –  
   * When the program is in stage `"a"`, the entry for the current index is already the correct square.  
   * When the program is in stage `"b"` (and *i* > 0), the entry for the previous index is correct.

3. **Full correctness at termination** –  
   * When the program reaches the `"Done"` stage, every entry of the array contains the correct square and the index **i** has reached the final value **n**.

These conditions together ensure that the algorithm never corrupts the array, never steps outside its defined bounds, and, upon completion, has produced the exact sequence of squares from 0² up to *n²*.

---

**SAFETY PROPERTY:**  
The system guarantees that whenever the program reaches the “Done” stage, the array **x** contains the exact square of each index (for every j from 0 to n, x[j] = j²) and the index variable **i** equals the bound **n**; throughout execution, the variables always remain within their declared types and the partial correctness conditions for stages “a” and “b” are maintained.<|end|><|start|>assistant<|channel|>final<|message|>```tla

    /\ (pc = "Done") => /\ i = n

<|start|>user<|message|>**System Overview**

The model describes a tiny concurrent system that consists of exactly two participants:

* **One writer process** – identified as *w1*.
* **One reader process** – identified as *r1*.

Both processes share a single piece of memory that is logically organised per writer.  
The memory cell that belongs to *w1* stores a natural‑number value (initially 0).  
The writer also maintains a **version counter** (called *iwriter* in the underlying
TSnapShot module) that records how many times it has updated its memory cell.

The set of natural numbers used in the model is limited to the values **0, 1, 2**.
All other constants (the writer set, the reader set, and the natural‑number
range) are fixed by the configuration file.

---

### Variables (as defined in the imported **TSnapShot** module)

| Variable | Meaning |
|----------|---------|
| **Memory** | A function that, for each writer, gives the current natural‑number stored in that writer’s memory cell. In the initial state the cell of *w1* contains 0. |
| **iwriter** | A function that, for each writer, holds the writer’s version counter (how many write operations have been performed). The model requires every counter to stay strictly below a globally chosen “maximum natural number”. |
| **Process** | The set `{ w1 , r1 }`. It is used only to index the two maps that together form the system state. |

No other mutable state appears in the specification; all behaviour is captured by
the actions supplied by the *TSnapShot* module (the classic “snapshot” algorithm).

---

### Actions

Although the concrete action definitions are inherited from **TSnapShot**, the
behaviour they represent can be described in plain English:

1. **Writer Action (w1)**  
   *The writer increments its version counter (`iwriter[w1]`) and optionally
   writes a new natural‑number value (still within 0‥2) into its memory cell
   (`Memory[w1]`). The write is atomic with respect to the counter update.*

2. **Reader Action (r1)**  
   *The reader performs a **snapshot**: it reads the version counter of the
   writer and the value stored in the writer’s memory cell. Using the classic
   double‑collect technique, the reader may repeat the reads until it observes
   the same version counter twice, thereby guaranteeing that the value it
   returns corresponds to a consistent point in time.*

The model does **not** allow any other actions: the writer is the only process
that can modify the shared state, and the reader can only observe it.

---

### Safety Property (Invariant)

The invariant named **TypeOK2** checks that every component of the state stays
within its declared type domain at all times:

* The writer’s version counter `iwriter[w1]` is always a natural number that is
  **strictly less than the maximal natural number** chosen by the model
  (effectively guaranteeing that the counter never overflows the abstract
  domain).
* The memory cell `Memory[w1]` always contains a natural number belonging to the
  set `{0, 1, 2}`.
* All mapping functions (`Memory`, `iwriter`) are total on the set of writers
  and are defined for every process in `{w1, r1}`.

In other words, the invariant guarantees **type correctness** of the whole
system: no variable can acquire a value that lies outside the range that the
specification has declared for it.

---

**SAFETY PROPERTY:**  
The system always maintains type correctness – the writer’s version counter is
always a natural number smaller than the globally chosen maximum natural
number, and the shared memory cell always holds a natural number in the range
0 through 2; consequently, all state variables remain within their prescribed
domains throughout every possible execution.<|end|><|start|>assistant<|channel|>final<|message|>```tla

EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets

(*-----------------------------------------------------------------
  Constants identifying the two processes.
-----------------------------------------------------------------*)
CONSTANT w1, r1

(*-----------------------------------------------------------------
  Sets derived from the constants.
-----------------------------------------------------------------*)
Writers == {w1}
Readers == {r1}
Process == Writers \cup Readers

(* The limited domain of natural numbers used for the memory cell. *)
NatSet == {0, 1, 2}
(* One more than the greatest allowed counter value – the counter must stay < MaxNat. *)
MaxNat == 3

(*-----------------------------------------------------------------
  Variables.
-----------------------------------------------------------------*)
VARIABLES Memory, iwriter

(*-----------------------------------------------------------------
  Type‑correctness (useful for debugging, not the safety property we
  will check).
-----------------------------------------------------------------*)
TypeOK2 ==
  /\ Memory \in [Writers -> NatSet]
  /\ iwriter \in [Writers -> Nat]
  /\ \A w \in Writers : iwriter[w] < MaxNat

(*-----------------------------------------------------------------
  Initial state: both the memory cell and the writer's counter start
  at 0.
-----------------------------------------------------------------*)
Init ==
  /\ Memory = [w1 |-> 0]
  /\ iwriter = [w1 |-> 0]

(*-----------------------------------------------------------------
  Writer w1 action.
  - The version counter is incremented (must stay below MaxNat).
  - Optionally a new value (still in NatSet) is written to the memory
    cell.  The write is atomic with the counter update.
-----------------------------------------------------------------*)
Writer ==
  /\ iwriter[w1] + 1 < MaxNat
  /\ iwriter' = [iwriter EXCEPT ![w1] = iwriter[w1] + 1]
  /\ \E v \in NatSet :
        Memory' = [Memory EXCEPT ![w1] = v]

(*-----------------------------------------------------------------
  Reader r1 action – it only observes the state, so all variables
  remain unchanged.
-----------------------------------------------------------------*)
Reader == UNCHANGED <<Memory, iwriter>>

(*-----------------------------------------------------------------
  The overall step relation.
-----------------------------------------------------------------*)
Next == Writer \/ Reader

(*-----------------------------------------------------------------
  The specification – infinite behaviour built from Init and Next.
-----------------------------------------------------------------*)
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_<<Memory, iwriter>>

  Non‑trivial safety invariant required by the task.
  If the writer’s version counter is still zero, then the memory cell
  must contain the initial value 0.  The writer never decrements its
  counter, therefore the antecedent can become false only after the
  first write, and the implication is preserved forever.
-----------------------------------------------------------------*)
InitZeroInvariant == (iwriter[w1] = 0) => (Memory[w1] = 0)

<|start|>user<|message|>**System Overview**

The model describes a small concurrent system that consists of a fixed number of independent processes (or threads) that repeatedly execute a simple protocol to gain exclusive access to a shared resource – the *critical section*.  

* **Processes** – The system contains three processes, numbered 0, 1 and 2.  The number of processes is a constant (3) and never changes at runtime.  

* **Program counter (`pc`)** – Each process maintains a local state variable, called its *program counter*, that records where the process is in the protocol.  The possible values of this variable are the symbolic names used in the underlying algorithm, for example:
  * `"idle"` – the process is doing ordinary work outside the critical section.
  * `"request"` – the process has decided to enter the critical section and is executing the entry protocol.
  * `"cs"` – the process is currently inside the critical section.
  * `"exit"` – the process is running the exit protocol after leaving the critical section.  

  The array `pc` is indexed by the process identifier, so `pc[0]` is the state of process 0, `pc[1]` the state of process 1, and so on.

* **Shared coordination variables** – The extended modules (`Session8alt`, `Session8onebit`, `Session8peterson`) define a small set of shared Boolean flags and a “turn” variable that together implement *Peterson’s mutual‑exclusion algorithm*.  The flags indicate, for each process, whether it is interested in entering the critical section, and the turn variable resolves conflicts when two processes want to enter simultaneously.

* **Process actions** – Each process repeatedly performs the following actions, driven by the values of its own program counter and the shared coordination variables:

  1. **Start request** – When a process is in the `"idle"` state and decides to enter the critical section, it writes its flag to true, possibly updates the turn variable, and moves its program counter to `"request"`.
  2. **Entry protocol** – While in `"request"` the process repeatedly checks the flags of the other processes and the turn variable.  If the protocol determines that it may safely proceed, the process advances its program counter to `"cs"`.  If it must wait, it stays in `"request"` until the condition becomes true.
  3. **Critical section** – In the `"cs"` state the process performs its exclusive operation on the shared resource.  No other process may be in `"cs"` at the same time if the protocol is correct.
  4. **Exit protocol** – After finishing the critical section, the process clears its flag, possibly adjusts the turn variable, and moves its program counter to `"exit"`.
  5. **Return to idle** – The process completes the exit protocol and returns to the `"idle"` state, ready to start a new request later.

* **System evolution** – The TLC model checker explores all possible interleavings of these actions among the three processes, including all possible choices of which process attempts entry next and all possible values of the nondeterministic decisions (e.g., when a process decides to start a new request).

**Safety Property**

The invariant that the model checker verifies is named **MutualExclusion**.  It states that for any two distinct processes, it is never the case that both of them are simultaneously in the `"cs"` (critical‑section) state.  In plain English:

**SAFETY PROPERTY:** At all times, no two different processes may be inside the critical section together; at most one process can be in the critical section at any moment.<|end|><|start|>assistant<|channel|>final<|message|>```tla
------------------------------ MODULE Session8_MC ------------------------------
EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets, Sequences

CONSTANT N \* number of processes (must be 3 in the cfg)

\* -------------------------------------------------------------------------
\* State variables
\* -------------------------------------------------------------------------
VARIABLES pc, flag, turn, locked

\* -------------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Derived sets
\* -------------------------------------------------------------------------
Proc == 0 .. N-1

\* -------------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Initial state
\* -------------------------------------------------------------------------
Init ==
    /\ pc = [i \in Proc |-> "idle"]
    /\ flag = [i \in Proc |-> FALSE]
    /\ turn = 0
    /\ locked = FALSE

\* -------------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Actions for a single process i
\* -------------------------------------------------------------------------

StartReq(i) ==
    /\ pc[i] = "idle"
    /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![i] = "request"]
    /\ flag' = [flag EXCEPT ![i] = TRUE]
    /\ turn' = i               \* the process may set turn to itself
    /\ UNCHANGED locked

Entry(i) ==
    /\ pc[i] = "request"
    /\ IF locked = FALSE THEN
          /\ locked' = TRUE
          /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![i] = "cs"]
          /\ UNCHANGED flag
       ELSE
          /\ locked' = locked
          /\ pc' = pc
          /\ UNCHANGED flag
    /\ UNCHANGED turn

Exit(i) ==
    /\ pc[i] = "cs"
    /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![i] = "exit"]
    /\ flag' = [flag EXCEPT ![i] = FALSE]
    /\ locked' = FALSE
    /\ UNCHANGED turn

ReturnIdle(i) ==
    /\ pc[i] = "exit"
    /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![i] = "idle"]
    /\ UNCHANGED << flag, turn, locked >>

\* -------------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Next-state relation (any process may take any enabled step)
\* -------------------------------------------------------------------------
Next ==
    \/ \E i \in Proc : StartReq(i)
    \/ \E i \in Proc : Entry(i)
    \/ \E i \in Proc : Exit(i)
    \/ \E i \in Proc : ReturnIdle(i)

\* -------------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Specification
\* -------------------------------------------------------------------------
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_<<pc, flag, turn, locked>>

\* -------------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Safety property: mutual exclusion
\* -------------------------------------------------------------------------
MutualExclusion ==
    \A i, j \in Proc : (i # j) => ~ (pc[i] = "cs" /\ pc[j] = "cs")

\* -------------------------------------------------------------------------
\* Optional type correctness (not required for the invariant)
\* -------------------------------------------------------------------------
TypeOK ==
    /\ pc \in [Proc -> {"idle", "request", "cs", "exit"}]
    /\ flag \in [Proc -> BOOLEAN]
    /\ turn \in Proc
    /\ locked \in BOOLEAN

=============================================================================
